name: Resilience
summary: The system recovers to a healthy state after disruption — it self-heals, degrades gracefully, and reprocesses affected data rather than staying broken.
description: Where fault tolerance is about surviving a failure in the moment, resilience is about the recovery afterward: returning to a correct, healthy state once the disruption passes. In data architectures this means replaying from a durable log, reprocessing idempotently so retries don't double-count, and degrading gracefully — serving stale-but-available results — while a component heals. Resilient designs favor patterns that make recovery routine and self-service: savepoints, circuit breakers, blue-green rollouts, and reruns.

mechanisms.name: Replay from log
mechanisms.note: Rewinding a durable, ordered log to reprocess any window of history after a bug fix, outage, or schema change.

mechanisms.name: Idempotent reprocessing
mechanisms.note: Designing writes so reprocessing the same records converges to the same result, making recovery safe to repeat.

mechanisms.name: Checkpoints and savepoints
mechanisms.note: Restoring streaming operators from a saved consistent snapshot so recovery resumes mid-stream instead of from scratch.

mechanisms.name: Circuit breakers and graceful degradation
mechanisms.note: Shedding load or serving cached/stale results when a dependency is unhealthy, keeping the system partially useful.

mechanisms.name: Blue-green and canary rollouts
mechanisms.note: Shifting traffic gradually to a new version so a bad deploy is rolled back before it degrades the whole platform.

mechanisms.name: Orchestrated reruns and backfills
mechanisms.note: Re-executing failed or corrected tasks from a known-good boundary so pipelines self-heal on the next scheduled run.

manifestations.statement: Because everything is a stream over a retained log, recovery is a first-class operation: rewind offsets, restore from a savepoint, and reprocess — a bad transform is fixed by replaying history, not by restoring backups.
Consumers rebuild their state by replaying the retained event log, and idempotent handlers make reprocessing safe, so a downstream service recovers simply by re-reading from a chosen offset.

Continuous commits plus a replayable source log let operators recover from savepoints and re-derive tables; time-travel snapshots make it easy to roll a table back to a healthy state after a bad batch.
Immutable bronze retains raw inputs, so silver and gold can be rebuilt idempotently after any downstream bug; table snapshots and time-travel let a corrupted layer be rolled back and reprocessed.
The batch layer periodically recomputes the authoritative view from scratch, self-healing any drift or corruption introduced by the speed layer — recovery is baked into the recomputation cadence.
Snapshot isolation and rollback let a bad commit be reverted atomically, and any engine can reprocess from an earlier snapshot, so recovery is a catalog operation rather than a restore.
Recovery is straightforward — rerun the job for the affected window — but reprocessing large windows is slow and may require careful cleanup if transforms weren't written idempotently.
dbt models rebuild deterministically from warehouse tables, so recovery is a rerun; incremental models, however, may need a full-refresh to heal cleanly after a defect, which can be expensive.
The raw/staging/marts split makes it clear where to rerun after a defect, and marts rebuild from staging; recovery still hinges on raw being retained and transforms being idempotent.
Buffered ingest and replayable logs help the platform catch up after connectivity gaps, but recovering device-side gaps depends on how long devices and the ingest tier retain unsent data.

Serving replicas recover by rebuilding from the source stream, but rebuilding large in-memory indexes takes time, so the system serves degraded freshness during recovery rather than instantly healing.
Replication resumes from the checkpointed log position after an outage; if the source log has rotated past that point, recovery requires a full re-snapshot rather than a graceful catch-up.

Insert-only satellites and hubs mean history is never overwritten, so recovering a bad load is a matter of reloading; the sprawling model, however, makes tracing and correcting the affected records laborious.
Recovery is constrained by downstream SaaS tools: replaying a sync can double-apply changes on non-idempotent endpoints, so healing a bad activation often needs manual reconciliation in each target.
With no materialized copy, there is nothing to reprocess or roll back — recovery is entirely a function of the underlying sources coming back healthy, which the federation layer cannot drive.
Recovery means re-running the single-process job by hand; there's no savepoint, replay log, or graceful degradation, so a disruption is resolved manually rather than by the system self-healing.
Once the on-prem link is restored the sync resumes, but there is often no automated catch-up or reconciliation, so operators must manually verify that no windows were skipped during the outage.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Resilience relies on spare capacity, redundant network paths, and multi-region standbys that sit idle in normal operation yet must be paid for continuously.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Retries, exponential backoff, and circuit-breakers protect the system under stress but add extra round-trips and waiting that slow the happy path even when nothing is failing.

tradeoffs.title: Operational complexity
tradeoffs.note: Self-healing controllers, savepoints, health probes, and chaos testing are demanding to design, validate, and keep working, adding significant engineering and operational burden.
